newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain doggedly pursues EMU but reception frosty.
newsitem.headline: Spain doggedly pursues EMU but reception frosty.

text.p: Spain has made fast progress in March to meet the economic requirements for Europe's common currency but the recognition it seeks for this work remains elusive.

Bolstered by solid economic news, Economy Secretary Cristobal Montoro on Friday said Spain -- once considered at best an outside shot -- was one of Europe's strongest candidates for the planned 1999 launch of the euro.

"We have been getting a series of good news which, together with the labour market reform agreement, builds confidence in Spain and confirms us as one of the strongest candidates for EMU launch," Montoro told journalists.
But despite the rapid progress, the market's assessment of Spain's chances has declined.
According to a Reuter survey of 45 economists published on Thursday, Spain's chances of joining the first wave were low and sinking further.

So far this month, Spain has reported that February inflation plunged, the Bank of Spain cut its key money market rate and unions and employers reached a rough agreement on labour reform designed to cut western Europe's worst unemployment rate.
More quietly, the Spanish peseta edged in wobbly, but unscathed fashion through the two-year anniversary of its last devaluation, on March 8, 1995.
Spain now tentatively meets the inflation and exchange rate criteria for economic and monetary union (EMU), in addition to long-term interest rates. Debt is too high but declining.

The sole remaining worry is the budget deficit, which the government has pledged to cut to three percent of gross domestic product from 4.4 percent in 1996 and 6.6 percent in 1995, noted bank BCH in a brokers' note.
"The participation of Spain in monetary union on January 1, 1999 now only depends on the fulfilment of three percent for the public deficit," BCH said.
Under EMU terms, Spain's inflation cannot exceed the 1997 average of the three best performers by more than 1.5 points.
In February, Spanish inflation slowed to 2.5 percent from 2.9 percent, abruptly fulfilling the euro inflation criteria for one month, government spokesman Miguel Angel Rodriguez said.

Economists argue that expectations for further drops should allow the overall inflation rate to average beneath 2.5 percent across the year, allowing Spain to meet this requirement -- once considered its toughest hurdle.
Exchange rates must observe normal fluctuation margins without severe tensions for two years.
"Really what's happened in the last week has definitely improved Spain's EMU chances," said Craig Schute, fixed-income economist at Bear Stearns in London.
In a statement, employers association CEOE also said the rate cut "helps clear up doubts about the peseta's entry into monetary union from the start of the project."
"The labour accord, lower inflation, the rate cut -- all of that is going to help Spain meet the fiscal target," Schute said.

The survey of economists found, however, that the negative market perception was largely because it was seen to be linked to the treatment of Italy, which is politically powerful as a Group of Seven nation but whose economic credentials are poorer than Spain's.
The survey, conducted on March 10 and 11, produced an averaged likelihood of only 18 percent that Spain would join the start -- down sharply from a 31 percent chance registered in February.
